newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan says Hun Sen agrees to peace talks with rival.
newsitem.headline: Japan says Hun Sen agrees to peace talks with rival.

text.p: Japan said on Sunday that Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen has agreed to open talks with forces of his rival, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, to end firece fighting in Phnom Penh.
A Japanese Foreign Ministry statement said the president of Cambodia's parliament, Chea Sim, told Japan's ambassador in Phnom Penh of the possible peace development in a meeting on Sunday.
It said the planned talks would involve Hun Sen, Chea Sim, a military representative of Prince Norodom Ranariddh, and First Vice-President Loy Simchheang, an ally of the prince.
Thousands of people fled the Cambodian capital on Sunday as heavy fighting raged for the second day running, with forces loyal to the rival prime ministers battling for power.
At least five people died, including a Japanese engineer who was brought to hospital critically wounded.
Japan, the biggest aid donor to Cambodia, has stepped in with a flurry of diplomatic activity to end the crisis and has urged Hun Sen to take the lead in finding a peaceful solution.

"Our nation is deeply concerned that the Cambodian situation had worsened. We strongly urge Second Prime Minister Hun Sen to take the initiative towards a peaceful resolution," Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said in a statement.
A Thai general said on Sunday he believed Hun Sen had effectively overthrown his rival, and reports from the city indicated that forces backing the second prime minister had the upper hand.
Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has ordered his embassy in Beijing to send a message to Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk -- who is also in Beijing -- asking him to help end the fighting.
"I have instructed a letter to be sent to King Sihanouk, asking for his cooperation," Hashimoto told reporters.
"If the two prime ministers show signs of compromise, King Sihanouk, now in Beijing, will be able to start efforts as a go-between," he said.
Hashimoto said he had also asked members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to urge the two leaders to end the fighting. Cambodia is due to join ASEAN this year.

Yukio Imagawa, Japan's special envoy to Cambodia, blamed Hun Sen's forces for the latest flareup. He recently returned from a meeting with the two prime ministers after an earlier outbreak of fighting on June 17.

"Fighting on June 17 could be called accidental, but this time Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's forces attacked First Prime Minister (Price Norodom) Ranariddh's forces with a deliberate military and political motive," Imagawa told Japan's Kyodo News on Sunday.
Imagawa said the weekend fighting was reminiscent of the 1970 coup which occured while then Prince Norodom Sihanouk was out of the country. The coup was followed by years of civil war.
"I hope a similar development won't happen this time," Imagawa said. The international community could not intervene because the matter was Cambodia's domestic affair, he added.

Imagawa visited Cambodia together with French special envoy Claude Martin last month to ask the two prime ministers to make mutual concessions and set a deadline for a national election. The election was scheduled to be held on May 23 next year.
Fighting broke out again on Saturday when Hun Sen, who opposes his rival's policy of negotiating with Khmer Rouge guerrillas, ordered a crackdown on "illegal troops" under Ranariddh's command.
The fighting intensified on Sunday with shelling and small arms fire rocking the capital. Explosions were heard in the city centre, near the palace and government buildings, a Reuters reporter said.
The Cambodian Red Cross said on Sunday that there had been 52 casualties from the fighting. It did not give a breakdown on the number of dead or wounded.
